rv.q: Towards the end, the play feels overloaded to the point of confusion. But it is still an original and entertaining piece, the shifts in mood beautifully managed by director Jack McNamara.
To go there with the obvious simile, its 90 minutes are like a grippingly unpredictable game of football – it’s just unfortunate that it ends without a satisfying result.
As a polemic, it needs greater dramatic development. Instead, Pringle falls back on footie-related bickering.
Pringle’s situation has great potential but the stretch after metaphor and relevance is strained, the characters too sketchily drawn and attempts at pathos heavy-handed.
It’s an admirably strange, haunting, and intellectually ambitious work from an exciting new voice in British theatre.
Complete extinction has seldom seemed so entertaining.
The Bounds isn't groundbreaking theatre. It is, however, a moving and punchy play that works well but struggles to find its feet style wise.

Reviewed at Royal Court theatre, London. In the sixteenth century football was a very different game. If what passed for football then can even be considered a game rather than a sprawling, brawling knot of teams from opposing villages, rucking forwards and backwards through woods and farmlands for hours with everyone playing in attack and, some...
As a whole, The Bounds is intellectually ambitious but too murky for its own sake.
But good performances can’t completely compensate for a plot that, like Gareth Southgate’s England squad, is apt to run out of puff in the closing minutes of the game.

cn.t: Pringle's Tudor football drama earns mixed reviews for its audacious premise and dark humor, though critics split on execution. Praised for ambition and timely themes, but some find it odd and uneven despite strong language and unsettling folk horror elements.
